title: Lefebvre's variations, No. 2 — on a theme by Wills: the lonely runner with four to seven runners, coprime speeds and no gap at the top
author: @Secousses
source: Special case of the lonely runner theorems for k ≤ 6 moving runners: U. Betke and J. M. Wills, Untere Schranken für zwei diophantische Approximations-Funktionen, Monatsh. Math. 76 (1972), 214–217, and T. W. Cusick, View-obstruction problems in n-dimensional Euclidean space and a generalization of them, Aequationes Math. 9 (1973) (k = 3); T. W. Cusick and C. Pomerance, View-obstruction problems III, J. Number Theory 19 (1984), 131–139 (k = 4); T. Bohman, R. Holzman and D. Kleitman, Six lonely runners, Electron. J. Combin. 8(2) (2001), R3, and J. Renault, View-obstruction: a shorter proof for 6 lonely runners, Discrete Math. 287 (2004) (k = 5); J. Barajas and O. Serra, The lonely runner with seven runners, Electron. J. Combin. 15 (2008), R48 (k = 6). Conjecture: J. M. Wills (1967), T. W. Cusick (1973). Origin of this statement: it is the missing step of a reduction of LonelyRunnerConjecture.classical_small_cases (LRC k for all k ≤ 6). The verified reduction proves LRC 0 directly, proves LRC 2 for coprime pairs (Wills, via the times j/(a+b)), proves a top-gap lemma (if LRC(k−1) holds and the largest speed is at least k times every other speed, a lonely time exists, by perturbing a lonely time of the k−1 smaller speeds), and divides any speed set by its gcd; the case left is exactly this statement.

title: Lefebvre's variations, No. 8 — on a theme by Adamczewski and Bugeaud: algebraic irrationals stay far from integers after multiplication by $b^{r+s}-b^r$ (the Diophantine step of Adamczewski–Bugeaud)
author: @Secousses
source: B. Adamczewski, Y. Bugeaud, On the complexity of algebraic numbers I. Expansions in integer bases, Ann. of Math. (2) 165 (2007), 547–565 (the proof of their combinatorial transcendence criterion applies the Subspace Theorem to exactly the points (b^{r+s}, b^r, p) and the linear forms above); B. Adamczewski, Y. Bugeaud, F. Luca, Sur la complexité des nombres algébriques, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 339 (2004), 11–14. The underlying theorems: H. P. Schlickewei, The p-adic Thue–Siegel–Roth–Schmidt theorem, Arch. Math. 29 (1977), 267–270 (p-adic Subspace Theorem; see also W. M. Schmidt, Diophantine Approximation, LNM 785, and Y. Bugeaud, Approximation by Algebraic Numbers, Cambridge Tracts in Math. 160, 2004, Chapter 2); D. Ridout, The p-adic generalization of the Thue–Siegel–Roth theorem, Mathematika 5 (1958), 40–48. Origin of this statement: it is the missing step of a reduction of BorelNormality.adamczewski_bugeaud_complexity (open milestone of BorelNormality.borel_conjecture). The reduction, verified in Lean, uses the pigeonhole principle on the p(n)+1 blocks of length n starting at positions 0..p(n), the identity floor(ξ b^(i+n)) = b^n floor(ξ b^i) + (value of the n digits at i), and the irrationality of ξ.

title: Lefebvre's variations, No. 7 — on a theme by Ramsey: $R(4,5)\le 25$ for graphs with all degrees in $[7,13]$
author: @Secousses
source: B. D. McKay and S. P. Radziszowski, R(4,5) = 25, J. Graph Theory 19 (1995), no. 3, 309–322 (computer-assisted proof that no graph on 25 vertices is K4-free with independence number at most 4; the statement here is that theorem restricted to graphs with all degrees in [7,13]). The lower bound R(4,5) ≥ 25 is due to J. G. Kalbfleisch, Construction of special edge-chromatic graphs, Canad. Math. Bull. 8 (1965) 575–584; the degree window comes from R(3,5) = 14 and R(4,4) = 18 (R. E. Greenwood and A. M. Gleason, Combinatorial relations and chromatic graphs, Canad. J. Math. 7 (1955) 1–7). Origin of this statement: it is the missing step of a reduction of RamseyValues.ramsey_four_five (R(4,5) = 25), a milestone of the mission RamseyValues.ramsey_five_five. That reduction proves R(3,5) ≤ 14 and R(4,4) ≤ 18 (Erdős–Szekeres recursion plus the Greenwood–Gleason parity step), deduces that every (4,5)-graph on 25 vertices has all degrees in [7,13], and proves R(4,5) ≥ 25 by checking the circulant graph on Z/24 with connection set {±1, ±2, ±4, ±8, ±9} by kernel evaluation.

title: Lefebvre's variations, No. 4 — on a theme by Schoenberg: Gegenbauer polynomials are positive definite on the sphere (Schoenberg)
author: @Secousses
source: I. J. Schoenberg, Positive definite functions on spheres, Duke Math. J. 9 (1942), 96–108 (positive definiteness of the Gegenbauer polynomials C_k^{((n-2)/2)} on S^{n-1}). Also: P. Delsarte, J.-M. Goethals, J. J. Seidel, Spherical codes and designs, Geom. Dedicata 6 (1977), 363–388; J. H. Conway and N. J. A. Sloane, Sphere Packings, Lattices and Groups, Chapter 9 and Chapter 13; E. M. Stein and G. Weiss, Introduction to Fourier Analysis on Euclidean Spaces, Chapter IV (addition theorem for zonal harmonics). The dimension-8 certificate f(t) = (t+1)(t+1/2)^2 t^2 (t-1/2) is from V. I. Levenshtein, On bounds for packings in n-dimensional Euclidean space, Soviet Math. Dokl. 20 (1979), 417–421, and A. M. Odlyzko and N. J. A. Sloane, New bounds on the number of unit spheres that can touch a unit sphere in n dimensions, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 26 (1979), 210–214. Origin of this statement: it is the missing step of a reduction of KissingNumber.kissing_number_eight (τ(8) = 240). In that reduction everything else is proved in Lean: the lower bound τ(8) ≥ 240 by the 240 roots of E8 (checked by kernel computation), and the upper bound τ(8) ≤ 240 by Delsarte's linear-programming argument with the Levenshtein polynomial, whose exact expansion f = 3/320 C_0 + 1/80 C_1 + 5/448 C_2 + 39/4480 C_3 + 19/3840 C_4 + 1/448 C_5 + 1/1792 C_6 in the polynomials C_k^{(3)} is verified by `ring`. The reduction uses the statement only for n = 8 and 1 ≤ k ≤ 6.

title: Lefebvre's variations, No. 21 — on a theme by Deuring: a supersingular elliptic curve over $\mathbb{F}_p$ for every prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$
author: @Secousses
source: M. Deuring, Die Typen der Multiplikatorenringe elliptischer Funktionenkörper, Abh. Math. Sem. Hansischen Univ. 14 (1941), 197–272 (existence of supersingular curves over F_p via reduction of CM curves). W. C. Waterhouse, Abelian varieties over finite fields, Ann. Sci. École Norm. Sup. (4) 2 (1969), 521–560, Theorem 4.1 (the trace t = 0 occurs over every prime field). R. Schoof, Nonsingular plane cubic curves over finite fields, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 46 (1987), 183–211, §4 (the number of F_q-isomorphism classes with trace t is the Kronecker class number H(t^2 − 4q); for t = 0, q = p this is H(−4p) > 0). J. H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, 2nd ed., Examples V.4.4 and V.4.5 (y^2 = x^3 + 1 for p ≡ 2 mod 3 and y^2 = x^3 + x for p ≡ 3 mod 4 are supersingular). C. Delfs and S. D. Galbraith, Computing isogenies between supersingular elliptic curves over F_p, Des. Codes Cryptogr. 78 (2016), 425–440, §2 (counts of F_p-rational supersingular j-invariants by class numbers). Origin of this statement: it is the missing step of a reduction of PrescribedPointCount.exists_isElliptic_trace_eq_of_dvd (Deuring's theorem over prime fields, supersingular case p | t). In that reduction everything else is proved in Lean: p | t and t^2 ≤ 4p force t = 0, or p ∈ {2, 3} and t = ±p; the count #E = 1 + #{affine solutions} for an elliptic curve and #E = q + 1 + Σ_x χ(x^3 + ax + b) for short Weierstrass curves in odd characteristic; y^2 = x^3 − x has p + 1 points for p ≡ 3 mod 4 (the character sum is odd under x ↦ −x) and y^2 = x^3 + 1 has p + 1 points for p ≡ 2 mod 3 (x ↦ x^3 is a bijection); the six remaining small cases over F_2 and F_3 (traces 0, ±2 over F_2 and ±3 over F_3) are explicit curves counted by decide. Only the primes p ≡ 1 mod 12 with t = 0 are left, and they are exactly this statement.

title: Lefebvre's variations, No. 23 — on a theme by Cohn and Elkies: Cohn–Elkies auxiliary functions reach the Kabatiansky–Levenshtein exponent (Cohn–Zhao)
author: @Secousses
source: H. Cohn and Y. Zhao, Sphere packing bounds via spherical codes, Duke Math. J. 163 (2014), no. 10, 1965–2002 (the Cohn–Elkies linear programming bound is always at least as strong as the Kabatiansky–Levenshtein bound; analogue of Rodemich's theorem). G. A. Kabatiansky and V. I. Levenshtein, Bounds for packings on a sphere and in space, Problems Inform. Transmission 14 (1978), 1–17 (Δ_d ≤ 2^{-(0.5990…+o(1))d}). H. Cohn and N. Elkies, New upper bounds on sphere packings I, Ann. of Math. 157 (2003), 689–714, Theorem 3.1 (the linear programming bound; on the platform as LinearProgrammingBound). H. Cohn, A conceptual breakthrough in sphere packing, Notices AMS 64 (2017). Origin of this statement: it is the missing step of a reduction of SpherePackingBeyond.kabatiansky_levenshtein (Δ_d ≤ 2^{-(0.599-ε)d} for all large d). In that reduction everything else is proved in Lean: a unit packing of Def_TenChallenges_SpherePacking is turned into a SpherePacking of separation 2 with literally the same density (so spherePackingConstant d ≤ SpherePackingConstant d, axiom-free), and the platform theorem LinearProgrammingBound (Cohn–Elkies), rewritten in real numbers, bounds SpherePackingConstant d by the ratio in item 4.

title: Lefebvre's variations: the zero set of a function changing sign across a rectangle contains a continuum crossing it
author: @Secousses
source: Classical planar topology. Continuous form of the Hex theorem: D. Gale, The game of Hex and the Brouwer fixed-point theorem, Amer. Math. Monthly 86 (1979), 818–827 (Hex theorem, equivalence with the Brouwer fixed point theorem in the plane); Steinhaus' chessboard theorem and its use for the Poincaré–Miranda theorem: W. Kulpa, The Poincaré–Miranda theorem, Amer. Math. Monthly 104 (1997), 545–550, and P. Tkacz, M. Turzański, An n-dimensional version of Steinhaus' chessboard theorem, Topology Appl. 155 (2008); crossing of paths joining opposite sides of a square from Brouwer's theorem: R. Maehara, The Jordan curve theorem via the Brouwer fixed point theorem, Amer. Math. Monthly 91 (1984), 641–643; separation in the square (unicoherence): K. Kuratowski, Topology, vol. II (1968), §61. Origin of this statement: it is the missing step of a reduction of SquarePeg.nielsen_wright_symmetric_curve (Nielsen–Wright, Rectangles inscribed in symmetric continua, Geom. Dedicata 56 (1995): every Jordan curve symmetric across a line or about a point inscribes a square). The verified reduction parametrizes the curve periodically and treats both symmetries with the lemma. Line symmetry (axis a + ℝu): it finds an excursion of the curve off the axis (parameters u0 < v0 with both ends on the axis, strictly on one side in between), applies the lemma on [u0, t*] × [t*, v0] (t* the first time of greatest distance to the axis) to F(s,t) = X(t) − X(s) (X the signed distance to the axis), and an intermediate value argument on the connected zero set gives two points at the same distance x ≠ 0 from the axis and 2x apart along it; with their mirror images they form a square. Point symmetry (centre z): it proves z is not on the curve (a closed-set and connectedness argument on the parameter interval), takes the last parameter at minimal distance to z and the next one at maximal distance, applies the lemma to F(s,t) = |γ(t) − z| − |γ(s) − z| on a rectangle whose top side ends at the antipode of the farthest point, and the intermediate value theorem for ⟨γ(s) − z, γ(t) − z⟩ on the connected zero set gives two points at the same distance from z in perpendicular directions, i.e. a square centred at z. Everything except the lemma is proved in Lean.

title: Lefebvre's variations: a finite witness that $|A-_GB|$ can exceed $\max(|A|,|B|,|A+_GB|)^{1.77898}$ (Lemm's sums–differences counterexample)
author: @Secousses
source: M. Lemm, New counterexamples for sums-differences, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 143 (2015), 3863–3868 (failure of SD(0,1,∞;α) for some α > 1.77898; bibliographic details to be checked against the mission source). Background: N. H. Katz, T. Tao, Bounds on arithmetic projections, and applications to the Kakeya conjecture, Math. Res. Lett. 6 (1999) 625–630; I. Z. Ruzsa's earlier counterexample with exponent log 6 / log 3. Origin of this statement: it is the missing step of a reduction of ArithmeticKakeya.lemm_sums_differences_barrier (open milestone of the mission ArithmeticKakeya.arithmetic_kakeya_1675). The reduction, verified in Lean, proves that every forcing constructible proof for X = {(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)} satisfies |S|^(n-t) ≤ N^(m+r) for every finite S ⊂ ℤ² with injective differences and |x·S| ≤ N (graph counting lemma via a log-concavity chain bound, plus injectivity of the forcing map), and applies it to a section of the difference map inside the witness G.
